steps.spokenScript: I'm assessing the neck — no JVD, no tracheal deviation, no tenderness or deformity noted.

steps.text: Chest

substeps.text: Inspects, palpates and assesses motor, sensory and distal circulatory functions (1 point/leg)

steps.spokenScript: I'm assessing the lower extremities bilaterally — no deformities, distal pulses present, sensation and motor function intact.

steps.text: Upper extremities

substeps.text: Inspects, palpates and assesses motor, sensory and distal circulatory functions (1 point/arm)

steps.spokenScript: I'm assessing the upper extremities bilaterally — no deformities, radial pulses present, sensation and motor function intact.

steps.text: Posterior thorax, lumbar and buttocks

substeps.text: Inspects and palpates lumbar and buttocks areas

steps.spokenScript: I'm assessing the posterior thorax, lumbar region, and buttocks — no tenderness, deformity, or abnormal findings noted.

steps.text: Manages secondary injuries and wounds appropriately
steps.spokenScript: I'm managing all secondary injuries and wounds — applying appropriate dressings and bandages as indicated.

steps.text: Demonstrates how and when to reassess the patient
steps.spokenScript: I'll reassess this patient every five minutes given their priority status, monitoring mental status, airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs en route.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to initiate or call for transport of the patient within 10 minute time limit
criticalCriteria.pearl: The examiner watches the clock from your first patient contact. 'Calling for transport now' — say it early. An unstable trauma patient is load-and-go; packaging continues en route. Ten minutes is shorter under pressure than in class.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to take or verbalize appropriate PPE precautions
criticalCriteria.pearl: Your very first words. Say 'taking BSI precautions' before you touch anything. This is the easiest point on the sheet — and the most commonly lost by candidates who glove up silently and assume the examiner noticed.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to determine scene safety
Failure to assess for and provide spinal protection when indicated
criticalCriteria.pearl: Mechanism drives the decision, not pain. High-speed crash, fall from height, or penetrating trauma near the spine — verbalize it: 'I'm maintaining spinal precautions.' You earn this point by saying it, not by automatically applying a collar.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to voice and ultimately provide high concentration oxygen
criticalCriteria.pearl: All trauma patients get high-flow O2 until proven otherwise. Say the device and the LPM: 'NRB at 15 LPM.' If you're managing an airway, state that BVM ventilation with 100% O2 is occurring. Silence fails you.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to assess/provide adequate ventilation
criticalCriteria.pearl: SpO2 < 90% or RR < 8 demands action, not documentation. Say 'I'm assisting ventilations with a BVM' and demonstrate it. Noting hypoxia without treating it is the most common way this criterion fails candidates.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to find or appropriately manage problems associated with airway, breathing, hemorrhage or shock
Failure to differentiate patient’s need for immediate transportation versus continued assessment/treatment at the scene
Performs other assessment before assessing/treating threats to airway, breathing and circulation
Failure to manage the patient as a competent EMT
criticalCriteria.pearl: The examiner's global competence catch. Think out loud: verbalize your reasoning, your interventions, and your reassessment. If your actions are protocol-driven and clinically sound, this criterion stays unchecked. Silence and hesitation invite it.

criticalCriteria.text: Exhibits unacceptable affect with patient or other personnel
Uses or orders a dangerous or inappropriate intervention

sheets.title: BVM Ventilation of an Apneic Adult Patient

steps.text: Takes or verbalizes appropriate PPE precautions
steps.spokenScript: I'm putting on gloves and eye protection.

steps.text: Checks responsiveness
steps.spokenScript: I'm checking responsiveness by tapping the shoulders and shouting — the patient is unresponsive.

steps.text: Requests additional EMS assistance
steps.spokenScript: I need additional EMS assistance — calling for backup now.

steps.text: Checks breathing and pulse simultaneously
steps.examinerNote: After checking responsiveness, then checking breathing and pulse for no more than 10 seconds, examiner informs candidate, “The patient is unresponsive, apneic and has a weak pulse of 60.”
steps.spokenScript: I'm simultaneously checking for breathing and a carotid pulse for no more than ten seconds — no pulse, no breathing detected.

steps.text: Opens airway properly
steps.examinerNote: The examiner must now inform the candidate, “The mouth is full of secretions and vomitus.”
steps.spokenScript: I'm opening the airway using a head-tilt chin-lift maneuver.

steps.text: Prepares rigid suction catheter
steps.spokenScript: I'm preparing and attaching the rigid suction catheter to the suction unit.

steps.text: Turns on power to suction device or retrieves manual suction device
steps.spokenScript: I'm turning on the power to the suction device and confirming it is functional.

steps.text: Inserts rigid suction catheter without applying suction
steps.spokenScript: I'm inserting the rigid suction catheter into the mouth without applying suction.

steps.text: Suctions the mouth and oropharynx
steps.examinerNote: The examiner must now inform the candidate, “The mouth and oropharynx are clear.”
steps.spokenScript: I'm applying suction and clearing the mouth and oropharynx — airway is now clear.

steps.text: Opens the airway manually
steps.spokenScript: I'm opening the airway manually using a head-tilt chin-lift.

steps.text: Inserts oropharyngeal airway
steps.examinerNote: The examiner must now inform the candidate, “No gag reflex is present and the patient accepts the airway adjunct.”
steps.spokenScript: I'm measuring and inserting an appropriately sized oropharyngeal airway.

steps.text: Ventilates the patient immediately using a BVM device unattached to oxygen
steps.note: Award this point if candidate elects to ventilate initially with BVM attached to reservoir and oxygen so long as first ventilation is delivered within 30 seconds.
steps.examinerNote: The examiner must now inform the candidate that ventilation is being properly performed without difficulty.
steps.spokenScript: I'm ventilating the patient immediately with the BVM unattached to oxygen, delivering one breath every five to six seconds with adequate chest rise.

steps.text: Re-checks pulse for no more than 10 seconds
steps.spokenScript: I'm rechecking for a carotid pulse for no more than ten seconds — no pulse detected.

steps.text: Attaches the BVM assembly [mask, bag, reservoir] to oxygen [15 L/minute]
steps.spokenScript: I'm attaching the BVM assembly to oxygen and setting the flow rate to fifteen liters per minute.

steps.text: Ventilates the patient adequately

substeps.text: Proper volume to cause visible chest rise

steps.examinerNote: The examiner must now ask the candidate, “How would you know if you are delivering appropriate volumes with each ventilation?”
steps.spokenScript: I'm continuing to ventilate the patient adequately — good chest rise with each breath.

criticalCriteria.text: After suctioning the patient, failure to initiate ventilations within 30 seconds or interrupts ventilations for greater than 30 seconds at any time
Failure to take or verbalize appropriate PPE precautions
criticalCriteria.pearl: BVM ventilation puts you face-to-face with aerosolized secretions. Gloves AND eye protection — verbalize both before you touch anything. 'PPE on, gloves and eye protection' is your opening line.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to suction airway before ventilating the patient
Suctions the patient for an excessive and prolonged time
Failure to check responsiveness, then check breathing and pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds
Failure to voice and ultimately provide high oxygen concentration [at least 85%]
Failure to ventilate the patient at a rate of 10 – 12/minute (1 ventilation every 5 – 6 seconds)
Failure to provide adequate volumes per breath [maximum 2 errors/minute permissible]
Insertion or use of any adjunct in a manner dangerous to the patient
Failure to manage the patient as a competent EMT
criticalCriteria.pearl: One breath every 5–6 seconds (10–12/min for adults), visible chest rise each time, minimal gastric distention, reassess position and seal constantly. Hyperventilation harms — set your rate and keep it. Show control, not urgency.

criticalCriteria.text: Exhibits unacceptable affect with patient or other personnel
Uses or orders a dangerous or inappropriate intervention

steps.text: Takes or verbalizes appropriate BSI/PPE precautions
Performs primary assessment and identifies respiratory distress
Verifies indications: SpO2 < 94%, increased work of breathing, suspected pulmonary edema or COPD exacerbation
Rules out contraindications: apnea, inability to follow commands, facial trauma, vomiting, BP < 90 mmHg systolic, respiratory rate < 8/min
Obtains patient cooperation and explains the procedure
Assembles CPAP unit and connects to O2 source at 10–15 LPM
Sets PEEP valve to appropriate pressure (typically 5 cm H2O per local protocol)
Selects correct mask size and applies snugly over nose and mouth
Secures mask with head straps, ensuring an adequate seal with no significant leak
Reassesses patient response: SpO2, work of breathing, mental status, and lung sounds
Adjusts PEEP or flow rate if patient deteriorates; prepares for BVM if CPAP fails
Documents intervention, device settings, and patient response

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to rule out contraindications before applying CPAP
criticalCriteria.pearl: Applying CPAP to a vomiting, apneic, or hypotensive patient can cause aspiration or worsen shock. State each contraindication check aloud — examiners need to hear your reasoning, not just watch you apply the mask.

criticalCriteria.text: Applies CPAP to an apneic or unresponsive patient
criticalCriteria.pearl: CPAP requires the patient to breathe spontaneously and protect their own airway. An unconscious patient needs a BVM, not CPAP. If the patient becomes unresponsive during treatment, remove the mask immediately and ventilate.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to reassess patient after CPAP application
criticalCriteria.pearl: CPAP can help or harm within minutes. Check SpO2, RR, mental status, and lung sounds at least once after application. If SpO2 drops or work of breathing worsens, the patient may need BVM or ALS backup.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to obtain patient cooperation before applying the mask
criticalCriteria.pearl: A panicked patient fighting the mask gets no benefit and risks injury. Take 30 seconds to explain what you’re doing. ‘This will make breathing easier — I need you to breathe with the mask.’ Compliance is part of the skill.

steps.text: Takes or verbalizes appropriate BSI/PPE precautions (gloves and eye protection)
Turns on suction device and confirms adequate suction (≥ 300 mmHg negative pressure)
Selects rigid Yankauer catheter for oral secretion suctioning
Measures catheter depth (corner of mouth to earlobe)
Pre-oxygenates patient for at least 30 seconds with 100% O2 if SpO2 and time allow
Positions patient: head-tilt or left lateral recumbent if unable to protect airway
Opens airway with head-tilt chin-lift (or jaw thrust if spinal injury suspected)
Inserts catheter to measured depth without applying suction
Applies suction while withdrawing catheter in a rotating motion; limits each attempt to 15 seconds
Re-oxygenates patient between suction attempts
Reassesses airway, breath sounds, SpO2, and level of consciousness
Documents findings, number of suction attempts, and patient response

criticalCriteria.text: Suctioning for longer than 15 seconds per attempt without re-oxygenating
criticalCriteria.pearl: Every second of suction removes both secretions and O2. Hypoxia can cause bradycardia and cardiac arrest in seconds. Set a mental or physical timer — 15 seconds max, then pull out and oxygenate before the next attempt.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to pre-oxygenate the patient before suctioning
criticalCriteria.pearl: Pre-oxygenation raises the O2 reserve so the brief hypoxia of suctioning doesn’t bottom out SpO2. Verbalize ‘100% O2 for 30 seconds’ before you reach for the catheter — especially in patients already hypoxic.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to reassess airway and SpO2 after suctioning
criticalCriteria.pearl: Suctioning can clear secretions or stimulate vasovagal bradycardia. Check breath sounds, SpO2, and mental status immediately after. If SpO2 dropped or rhythm changed, report it and manage it.

criticalCriteria.text: Applying suction while inserting the catheter
criticalCriteria.pearl: Suction on insertion creates mucosal trauma and can pull tissue into the catheter tip. Insert to depth with suction off, then apply suction only while withdrawing. This is a technique point examiners watch closely.

steps.text: Takes or verbalizes appropriate BSI/PPE precautions
Positions patient comfortably seated or supine
Locates radial pulse with 2–3 fingertips at the wrist
Counts pulse for at least 30 seconds and multiplies by 2 (or full 60 seconds if irregular)
Assesses and reports rate, rhythm (regular/irregular), and quality (strong/weak/thready)
Selects appropriate BP cuff size and applies it 1 inch above the antecubital fossa
Estimates systolic pressure by palpation: inflates cuff until radial pulse disappears, then adds 30 mmHg
Places stethoscope bell or diaphragm over brachial artery
Deflates cuff at 2–3 mmHg/second; records systolic (first Korotkoff sound) and diastolic (sounds cease)
Reports blood pressure accurately in mmHg (systolic/diastolic)
Assesses respirations without alerting patient (may keep fingers on wrist after pulse check)
Counts breaths for at least 30 seconds and multiplies by 2
Assesses and reports rate, rhythm, and depth (shallow/normal/deep)
Applies pulse oximeter probe to appropriate digit or site
Waits for stable waveform and reports SpO2 percentage

criticalCriteria.text: Reporting inaccurate vital signs (off by more than acceptable range)
criticalCriteria.pearl: Accuracy matters clinically and on the exam. Practice until you can reliably land within ±4 mmHg on BP and ±2/min on pulse/RR. Examiners use a reference patient — report what you actually hear, never guess.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to assess all required vital signs (pulse, BP, and respirations at minimum)
criticalCriteria.pearl: Skipping one vital sign fails this station. Even if SpO2 is unavailable, pulse + BP + RR are mandatory. Make it a habit to verbalize each finding as you complete it so the examiner can score you.

criticalCriteria.text: Alerting the patient before counting respirations
criticalCriteria.pearl: Telling a patient you’re watching their breathing immediately changes it. Transition seamlessly from pulse check — keep your fingers on the wrist and watch the chest. Examiners will note if you announce the respiration count.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to use proper technique for auscultated blood pressure
criticalCriteria.pearl: Palpated BP (systolic only) is a field skill; the exam requires auscultation for both systolic and diastolic. Inflate 30 mmHg above the palpated estimate, release slowly, and listen for both Korotkoff sounds.

steps.text: Takes or verbalizes appropriate BSI/PPE precautions
Explains procedure to patient and positions supine
Exposes chest; preps skin (clean/dry; clip or shave hair if needed for electrode contact)
Applies RA (white) electrode to right arm — wrist or forearm
Applies LA (black) electrode to left arm — wrist or forearm
Applies RL (green) electrode to right leg — ankle or lower leg (ground lead)
Applies LL (red) electrode to left leg — ankle or lower leg
V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border
V4: 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line (place V4 before V3)
V3: Between V2 and V4 (diagonal, on 4th–5th ICS)
V5: Anterior axillary line at the same level as V4
V6: Midaxillary line at the same level as V4 and V5
Instructs patient to lie still and breathe normally; acquires 12-lead tracing
Reviews tracing for artifact; re-applies any lead with poor contact
Identifies STEMI pattern or transmits tracing to receiving facility per protocol

criticalCriteria.text: Reversing limb leads (LA/RA or LL/RL swap)
criticalCriteria.pearl: Reversed limb leads produce a mirror-image artifact that mimics dextrocardia or masks ST changes. The examiner will check lead placement, not just the tracing. Color-code in your memory: white on right, black on left, green on right leg.

criticalCriteria.text: Incorrect placement of one or more precordial leads
criticalCriteria.pearl: Off by one intercostal space changes the ST segment appearance dramatically — a false STEMI or a missed one. Landmark V1 at the 4th ICS by counting ribs, place V4 at the midclavicular 5th ICS, then fill in V3 between them.

criticalCriteria.text: Failure to identify or communicate a STEMI pattern
criticalCriteria.pearl: STEMI recognition is the clinical reason for the 12-lead. ≥1 mm ST elevation in two contiguous leads, or ≥2 mm in V1–V4, is a cath-lab activation. Verbalize your finding — ‘I see ST elevation in V1–V4, activating cath lab per protocol.’

criticalCriteria.text: Acquiring a tracing with excessive artifact without correcting it
criticalCriteria.pearl: Wandering baseline and muscle artifact make interpretation impossible. Instruct the patient to lie still, check for poor electrode contact, and re-acquire. A tracing you can’t read is clinically worthless.
